sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML text, Else et al. 2022)

steps.action: Collated published sea ice TA:TIC ratios and TIC/TA concentrations showing wide between-study variability.
steps.quote: Published results have reported ratios spanning 0.9 to 2.2 from a variety of different Arctic and Antarctic field sites

steps.action: Took up the sea ice pump theory in which ikaite precipitation enriches bulk ice in TA relative to TIC.
steps.quote: The hypothesized cause of this TA enrichment was the precipitation of ikaite

steps.action: Posed the question of how differing physical and biological processes shape horizontal and vertical carbonate distributions and whether they alter bulk TA and TIC used in models.
steps.quote: This paper seeks to contrast the two sites with objectives to characterize how differing physical and biological processes impact both horizontal and vertical distributions

steps.action: Relied on the authors' earlier establishment of an invisible polynya with strong currents, thinner ice and higher algae between the Finlayson Islands.
steps.quote: Our study builds on work conducted by Dalman et al. (2019), who described an invisible polynya between the islands.

steps.action: Selected a polynya site (POLY) and a thick first-year ice site (TFYI) 7 km apart, using the natural contrast as a natural laboratory.
steps.quote: we selected two level ice sites (Fig. 1) based on Dalman et al. (2019)

steps.action: Designed a statistical sampling scheme of five random cores per site per date (15 per horizon per site) sampled at top, middle and bottom 10 cm, plus one high-resolution core per site.
steps.quote: we designed a statistical sampling method in which on each date, five locations were randomly selected within a 10 m radius

steps.action: Measured under-ice currents, snow depth, ice thickness, ice temperature and bottom-ice Chl a at both sites.
steps.quote: The polynya site, POLY, experienced considerably higher under-ice currents

steps.action: Compared algal biomass with the earlier Dalman et al. (2019) pattern and found the opposite, with higher biomass at TFYI.
steps.quote: In contrast to the results of Dalman et al. (2019), bottom-ice algal biomass was about 3 times higher at TFYI than at POLY

steps.action: Measured high-resolution TIC, TA and salinity profiles at both sites on 10 May.
steps.quote: The polynya site was characterized by “c-shaped” profiles for TIC, TA, and salinity

steps.action: Calibrated the TIC and TA analysers against certified reference material and reported precision (Methods check supporting the carbonate measurements).
steps.quote: Both instruments were calibrated prior to measurement using certified reference material (CRM batch no. 177)

steps.action: Checked the single-core profile pattern against the 15-core statistical samples, which reproduced the top and bottom divergence.
steps.quote: they confirm the general patterns observed in Fig. 4

steps.action: Tested the null of equal site means by ANOVA per horizon: top and bottom differed significantly, the middle did not.
steps.quote: The middle horizon was statistically indistinguishable between the two sites for all three parameters.

steps.action: Set enhanced ocean heat flux against deep snow as rival causes of the thinner polynya ice, and used thermodynamic model expectations to apportion about half to snow.
steps.quote: Melling et al. (2015) also hypothesized deep snow as a potential cause of invisible polynyas

steps.action: Checked whether the snow and ice difference was a small-scale drift artifact using an independent 4.5 km snow and ice transect.
steps.quote: the long transect conducted on 12 May (Fig. 5) shows a consistent pattern of deeper snow and thin ice

steps.action: Reconstructed freeze-up from AMSR2 sea ice concentration maps and excluded differing consolidation timing as a cause of the snow and ice differences.
steps.quote: Maps of sea ice concentration that we acquired for the freeze-up season show that ice at the two sites consolidated at roughly the same time

steps.action: Revised the expectation of current-boosted algae at POLY, attributing the reversed algal pattern to light limitation under thick snow.
steps.quote: it is most likely that light limitation under thick snow at the polynya site overshadowed any potential boost in production

steps.action: Proposed rivals for higher top-horizon salinity at POLY: faster initial growth, turbulence-driven frazil formation, and early-season flooding.
steps.quote: another explanation is that ice formation at the two sites occurred under different turbulence conditions

steps.action: Compared the salinity standard deviation with Weeks and Lee (1962) criteria to support the turbulent-formation interpretation.
steps.quote: the standard deviation of salinity we observed was indeed much higher at the polynya site (1.2) than the thick first-year ice site (0.4)

steps.action: Derived the conservative brine-rejection expectation as a mixing line between pure ice and the seawater reference endmember.
steps.quote: a mixing line between a pure ice endmember (salinity, TIC, TA = 0 ) and our reference seawater endmember

steps.action: Compared bulk TIC and TA against the mixing line: middle and bottom samples follow it, top samples fall well below it.
steps.quote: the top core sections are substantially lower (for both TIC and TA) than the mixing line

steps.action: Excluded ikaite precipitation alone as the cause of surface depletion, because the TIC:TA depletion ratio is opposite to its stoichiometry.
steps.quote: precipitation alone would result in TA being twice as depleted as TIC, and what we observed is the opposite

steps.action: Kept CO2 gas evasion as the primary explanation for surface TIC loss, with ikaite as a secondary contributor to TA depletion.
steps.quote: Gas evasion is a strong candidate for explaining large depletions in TIC

steps.action: Derived from growth-rate and salinity theory and from Feltham et al. (2002) the expectation of lower middle-horizon salinity, TA and TIC at POLY.
steps.quote: We therefore anticipated lower salinity and perhaps lower TA and TIC in the polynya ice

steps.action: Compared the expectation with the ANOVA results for the middle horizon; the expectation failed.
steps.quote: Table 3 shows that our expectations were not met

steps.action: Refined the growth-rate account: estimated middle-horizon growth rates of about 0.6 vs 0.7 cm/d and proposed that this difference is too small to matter.
steps.quote: We hypothesize that large differences in initial growth rates compared to later winter growth rates are enough to produce significant vertical variations in salinity

steps.action: Compared bottom-horizon chemistry with the expected biological TIC drawdown; found higher TIC at the higher-algae site, explained by salinity.
steps.quote: This counterintuitive result is explained again by salinity

steps.action: Salinity-normalized TIC and TA and fitted nTA vs nTIC regression slopes per site and horizon, for comparison with process stoichiometries (photosynthesis, CaCO3, gas exchange).
steps.quote: we normalized TIC and TA values to the estimated seawater endmember salinity

steps.action: Compared fitted slopes (0.50 to 1.03) with the photosynthesis/respiration slope and found no match, even at the bottom.
steps.quote: they do not follow the photosynthesis line, even in the bottom ice horizon (Table 4)

steps.action: Re-examined slopes for the bottom horizon alone, because pooled slopes are biased by equal sampling of thin layers.
steps.quote: It may, however, be more instructive to consider the slope of the bottom horizon alone (Table 4)

steps.action: Kept a minor biological role at the bottom, with a shift towards net respiration (net heterotrophy) under weak ice algal production.
steps.quote: suggesting a shift towards the net respiration line

steps.action: Compared middle and bottom TA:TIC (~1.05) with the seawater ratio and with the original sea ice pump reports of ratios approaching 2:1.
steps.quote: not meaningfully different from our estimate of the source seawater TA : TIC ratio (1.04)

steps.action: Kept the claim that ikaite precipitates in the study area but in amounts too small to fractionate TA and TIC.
steps.quote: ikaite precipitation certainly seems to be occurring in our study area

steps.action: Computed vertically weighted average TIC, TA and TA:TIC for each site (differences of 2.0 to 4.6 %).
steps.quote: when a weighted vertical average of the two sites is calculated, the carbonate chemistry (particularly the TA : TIC ratio) is not meaningfully different

steps.action: Kept the conclusion that brine drainage dominates sea ice carbonate chemistry, and suggested deriving an empirical salinity and source-water relation for models.
steps.quote: these processes were dominated by brine drainage processes as evidenced by strong relationships with salinity

sequences.source_document: Open discussion tc-2021-320 (RC1, AC1, RC2, AC2 and supplements)

steps.action: Both referees asked for horizon-specific regressions in Fig. 8; the authors computed slopes per horizon and site and added a new Table 4.
steps.quote: I suggest making separate regression lines for each layer for the 2 cores

steps.action: Revised the biology conclusion in the abstract and Sect. 4.4 from no noticeable impact to a minor control with net heterotrophy.
steps.quote: biology appeared to exert only a minor control, with some evidence that the ice algae community was net heterotrophic

steps.action: Added the permeability mechanism of Moreau et al. (2015) for surface CO2 outgassing.
steps.quote: this paper does present a good discussion of the controls of outgassing

steps.action: Rephrased the summary of earlier model studies so that deep-convection regions are not misrepresented.
steps.quote: That sentence did leave the wrong impression.

steps.action: Replaced the erroneous Table 2, which duplicated Table 1, with the biogeochemical data table.
steps.quote: Wow, we are very sorry about that. The updated table should be as follows

steps.action: Added surface flooding as a rival explanation for higher top-horizon salinity, TIC and TA at POLY.
steps.quote: It’s plausible enough to be worth mentioning.

steps.action: Added an auxiliary note that ikaite dissolves during room-temperature melting, so the method measures total inorganic carbon.
steps.quote: At room temperature, ikaite crystals are highly unstable and dissolve back into the meltwater

steps.action: Refined the ikaite claim to say that crystals are lost to seawater at a rate similar to brine rejection.
steps.quote: ikaite crystals are lost to the underlying seawater at a similar rate to brine rejection

steps.action: Revised the statement linking the current increase to tidal amplitude predictions.
steps.quote: Good point, we revised this statement to improve clarity

steps.action: Added a quantitative comparison with the Chl a biomass and snow thickness reported by Dalman et al. (2019).
steps.quote: with an average snow thickness of 2.8 +/- 0.5 cm

steps.action: Built per-date tables, placed in the supplement, showing that ice chemistry was stable between sampling dates.
steps.quote: it does help show that the ice chemistry was quite stable between sampling dates

steps.action: Declined the request to reorder the methods paragraphs on core sampling.
steps.quote: We did find this section a little difficult to organize but prefer the current structure.

end.claim: Carbonate chemistry at both sites was dominated by brine drainage (tracking salinity), with site differences confined to thin top and bottom layers, so vertically averaged TIC, TA and TA:TIC did not differ meaningfully between polynya and non-polynya ice.

decisive_move.sentence: The statistical sampling design (15 random cores per horizon per site) made the ANOVA comparison possible; without it the horizon-by-horizon site differences and the null middle-horizon result could not be established against core-to-core heterogeneity.

gates.evidence: Sites were chosen from the prior Dalman et al. (2019) finding of contrasting currents, ice and algae, with stated expectations (§2.1 ¶2). The sampling design and ANOVA null were set before analysis (§2.2 ¶4, §2.4 ¶1). The middle-horizon expectation of lower salinity at POLY was stated and failed (§4.3 ¶1), and ANOVA could have shown bulk differences. Nothing was preregistered, and most process attributions are post hoc.

novelty_claims.quote: To our knowledge, the present study is the first attempt to employ a statistical sampling approach to compare sea ice carbonate chemistry between two sites.
to our knowledge this has not been investigated in any detail in past studies

limits: Sub-claim statuses: significant top and bottom site differences = confirmed (ANOVA, Table 3); middle-horizon equivalence = regularity_in_range (one season, two sites); gas evasion at the surface = best_explanation; ikaite present but minor = best_explanation (no microscopy or XRD, §4.5 ¶3); net heterotrophy at the bottom = weak best_explanation (n = 3 Chl a pools); about half of the thinner polynya ice attributed to snow = rough estimate; frazil and turbulence origin of the top layer = untested (no thin sections, §4.2 ¶1). The paper does not show: under-ice seawater sampled at the time (reference built from summer 2016-2019 data, n = 5); interannual replication (the algae reversal versus Dalman et al. is unresolved); any test of the proposed salinity-to-carbonate empirical relation. The review record shows that the per-horizon slope analysis (Table 4) and the net-heterotrophy interpretation were added at referee request; the final_paper sequence codes these from the published text alone as author steps. Inference: the methods sentence on ikaite dissolution during melting promised in AC1 does not appear in the published §2.2. Composition trace_series fits loosely: only two sites, found rather than set, with rivals weighed after the data.

disagreements.target: Dalman et al. (2019), higher bottom-ice algal biomass in the polynya
disagreements.support: New Chl a sampling at the same sites found about three times higher biomass at TFYI, attributed to light limitation under thicker snow at POLY.
disagreements.quote: In contrast to the results of Dalman et al. (2019), bottom-ice algal biomass was about 3 times higher at TFYI than at POLY

disagreements.target: Rysgaard et al. (2007), bulk TA:TIC ratios approaching 2:1 as evidence for the sea ice pump
disagreements.support: Middle and bottom ratios near 1.05 match the seawater ratio of 1.04; ikaite is present but too small to fractionate TA and TIC.
disagreements.quote: the majority of studies since have reported values close to 1 : 1 below the surface ice layers

disagreements.target: Modelling studies prescribing a single TA:TIC ratio of 2:1 (Rysgaard et al., 2011; Grimm et al., 2016; Mortenson et al., 2018)
disagreements.support: The weighted averages support a single bulk value, but at a ratio near 1:1 that varies regionally with source water and salinity.
disagreements.quote: a single TA : TIC ratio, typically 2 : 1

disagreements.target: Community position that spatial heterogeneity explains divergent reports of sea ice carbonate chemistry
disagreements.support: Sites chosen as extremes of spatial variability gave near-identical vertically averaged chemistry.
disagreements.quote: suggests that we should perhaps be looking at other factors (perhaps methodologies) to explain divergent reports

disagreements.target: Growth-rate and salinity relationships and the Feltham et al. (2002) current-enhanced brine drainage prediction
disagreements.support: The predicted lower middle-horizon salinity at the polynya was not observed; the authors attribute this to small mid-winter growth-rate differences.
disagreements.quote: Table 3 shows that our expectations were not met

disagreements.target: Past attribution of low bottom-ice TIC to algal drawdown (Brown et al., 2015; Delille et al., 2007)
disagreements.support: The higher-algae site had higher bottom TIC, explained by salinity, with slopes off the photosynthesis line.
disagreements.quote: These lower values are typically attributed to biological drawdown caused by the bottom-ice algal bloom.
